course.title: ML Hybrid Course
course.lead: One ordered path from an empty Python prompt to AGI arguments, built out of the books and notes already on this laptop and split into day-sized lessons. Days 1-8 teach Python from nothing, Days 9-17 teach the mathematics from nothing, Days 18-33 build classical machine learning, Days 34-38 do it again in a practitioner's hands-on account, and Days 39-85 run the AGI track: Togelius on what generality even means, the OpenCog architecture survey, context engineering, agentic coding, edge deployment, a second pass on AGI theory, and a closing gate on governance as architecture. Each day names the book, the exact pages, the author's own words at bite size, one local exercise, and an automatic spaced review of the days you already completed. You never re-open a book from page one.
course.method: Kumon-style rhythm, borrowed from the local developer path: **recall** (5 min, from memory) -> **read the author** (10-15 min, one bite) -> **practice** (20-30 min, one local exercise) -> **check** (5 min, run it and log the correction). Move on only when you can explain the idea without looking. Review re-tests earlier days at 1, 3, 7 and 21 lessons back, automatically. Structure grafted from the local SyncSenta teacher curriculum (`Sync-0.0.2/data/ai_curriculum.json`): every sub-strand carries learning outcomes, prerequisites, expected misconceptions and assessment evidence - those four fields are what the days below use as `idea`, `recall`, `misconception` and `check`. Not KICD/CBC-aligned; a personal adaptation.

days.title: Why Python is chapter one of this course
days.idea: Python is the machine you will think in for the next 84 days: an interpreter you can type at, a standard library that already contains most of what you need, and no compile step between an idea and a result.
days.recall: From memory: name three things Python is used for in the books on this laptop, and one thing it is not good at.
days.misconception: Believing you must finish a whole Python book before touching machine learning. You need eight days of it, not eight weeks - and the rest you learn against a real exercise.
days.practice: Read `../python-exercises/README.md`, then run `python3 python-exercises/run_tests.py` from `~/Desktop/ex/exercises`. The exercises should fail with a TODO, not with an import error. That red board is your starting line, so write down which ones failed.
days.check: Say out loud what an interpreter does with one line of code, and what `>>>` means. Both sentences go in your log before this day is complete.
days.gate: Run three lines at the Python prompt and explain what each one printed, including the one that printed nothing.

days.title: Python as a calculator, then as a language
days.idea: Everything else grows out of expressions: values, operators, and the rule that a program is evaluated one statement at a time, top to bottom.
days.recall: From memory: the difference between an expression and a statement, and what `%` does.
days.misconception: Believing `3 / 2` and `3 // 2` are the same, or that a large literal silently becomes a float. They are three different operators with three different answers.
days.practice: `../python-exercises/exercises/00_foundations/01_tip_total.py` - arithmetic, arguments and validation. Run it, make it fail, make it pass, and only then read the matching solution.
days.check: Cold-write the one-sentence idea of today plus your own example of an expression that is not a statement.
days.gate: Compute an 18% tip on 47.35 to the cent without looking, then explain why you rounded the way you did instead of truncating.

days.title: Variables, types, and what a name actually binds
days.idea: A variable is a name bound to an object that carries its own type; the four primitives (integer, float, boolean, string) cover almost all the arithmetic a model does before you reach for arrays.
days.recall: From memory: name the four primitive types, and one operation that changes type rather than raising an error.
days.misconception: Thinking `x = 5` makes `x` an integer forever, or that `"5" + 2` is a bug in Python rather than a rule about what `+` means for strings.
days.practice: `../python-exercises/exercises/00_foundations/02_grade_band.py` - conditions and boundary cases. Write your own boundary table (0, 49, 50, 100) on paper before you code it.
days.check: Explain in one sentence what `type()` would answer for each primitive, and why the boolean is the odd one out.
days.gate: Predict, then run, the type and value of six expressions you wrote yourself. Every wrong prediction becomes a repeat of this day, not a note.

days.title: Choosing a container: list, tuple, dict, set
days.idea: Four built-in containers answer four different questions - order, immutability, lookup by key, membership - and most beginner bugs are a container chosen for the wrong question.
days.recall: From memory: which container keeps insertion order, which cannot be changed afterwards, and which one you would reach for to count words.
days.misconception: Reaching for a list when the real question is 'have I seen this before?' - that is a set, and the list version is secretly quadratic.
days.practice: `../python-exercises/exercises/01_collections/04_word_counts.py`, then `05_median.py`. Both must pass on your own attempt before you open the solutions.
days.check: Write the one-line rule for each of the four containers from memory, then check all four against the pages.
days.gate: Given a log of student scores, say which container you would use at each step and why, out loud, in under a minute.

days.title: Control flow: the order the machine really runs things in
days.idea: Conditionals select, loops repeat, and the indentation *is* the block - Python has no braces, so the layout you can see is the structure that executes.
days.recall: From memory: what a `for` loop does on its last element, and when you would write `while` instead.
days.misconception: Reading `if` and `for` as decoration. A loop meant to run 30 times that runs 29 is an off-by-one you can see, not bad luck.
days.practice: `../python-exercises/exercises/00_foundations/03_is_prime.py`, then `06_flatten.py` - recursion is control flow with a stack, and it belongs next to loops.
days.check: Trace one loop by hand for n = 7, writing the value of the counter at every pass. The trace goes in your log with the code.
days.gate: Explain why testing divisors from 2 differs from testing from 1, and why both are still too slow past the square root.

days.title: Functions: the unit of reusable thought
days.idea: A function names a piece of reasoning once so you can call it forever; parameters, a return value, and a one-line docstring are the whole interface you owe the future reader.
days.recall: From memory: the difference between printing inside a function and returning from it.
days.misconception: Passing state through globals because it saves a keystroke, then finding you cannot run the same function twice and get the same answer.
days.practice: `../python-exercises/exercises/02_data/07_parse_scores.py` and `08_safe_int.py` - both are function-writing exercises about data you do not trust.
days.check: Write the signature - name, parameters, return type - of the function you just wrote, before you look at its code again.
days.gate: Refactor one earlier exercise into a function that takes an argument and returns a value with no `print` inside it, and show that it still passes.

days.title: NumPy: why machine-learning code does not use lists
days.idea: NumPy replaces a list of boxed Python objects with one flat typed buffer plus vectorised operations, which is why an entire column can be scaled in a single line.
days.recall: From memory: two things an array does that a list cannot, and one thing a list still does better.
days.misconception: Believing you must have NumPy installed to understand the idea. It is **not** installed on this laptop and there is no pip here, so the concept is carried by the loop you write by hand - which is the point of the exercise.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/02_standardize.py` - do the whole thing with plain lists first, then write the one-line vectorised version you wish you had as pseudocode in your log.
days.check: Say in one sentence what 'vectorised' means, and name where the loop went.
days.gate: Explain to your Day 1 self why subtracting the mean works on a whole column at once.

days.title: pandas: the table as an interface
days.idea: A DataFrame is a dictionary of equal-length columns with labels, and most of the data-cleaning vocabulary of machine learning - slice, join, group, fill - is a table operation rather than an algorithm.
days.recall: From memory: name three things you would do to a messy CSV before any model is allowed to see it.
days.misconception: Thinking pandas is required for this course. It is not installed here; the standard-library `csv` path in `../ml-exercises` covers the same skills, and the consolidation day makes you do it that way on purpose.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` - read a small CSV you write yourself with `csv.DictReader`, then split rows into train and test with a fixed seed so the split repeats.
days.check: Write the three verbs (select, filter, aggregate) with one example of each taken from the code you just ran.
days.gate: Explain what an index is, and what goes wrong when two tables with different indexes are combined.

days.title: Logical formulas: reading a claim precisely
days.idea: A formula has truth values, not moods. And, or, not, implies and if-and-only-if let you write a claim once and check it mechanically - including the contrapositive you will need in every debugging session.
days.recall: From memory: write `p implies q` and its contrapositive, and say exactly when each is false.
days.misconception: Reading 'if p then q' as 'if q then p'. Confusing an implication with its converse is the root of most arguments about metrics.
days.practice: Author a short standard-library script in your log folder that builds the truth tables for `p implies q`, `q implies p` and `not q implies not p`, then prints which columns agree. This exercise is yours, so it is the one thing on this day you may not skip.
days.check: Cold-write the five connectives in symbols and in English, one line each.
days.gate: Take one claim from Day 8 - 'if a column is numeric then I can average it' - state its contrapositive and its converse, then say which of the two is true.

days.title: Mathematical data types: sets, sequences, functions, relations
days.idea: The same four objects carry all later maths: a set of cases, a sequence of measurements, a function from inputs to outputs, and a relation that may pair one input with many outputs.
days.recall: From memory: the difference between a function and a relation, and between a sequence and a set.
days.misconception: Calling a model 'a function' while treating its output as a set of plausible answers. That slip is exactly what an evaluation metric exists to settle.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` again, now read as a partition: show that the two sets are disjoint and that their union is the whole dataset.
days.check: Write the domain, codomain and range of the splitting function you just tested.
days.gate: Describe your Day 6 safe-conversion function in domain-and-codomain terms, naming the input it must refuse.

days.title: Induction: why ten passing tests still prove nothing
days.idea: Induction proves an infinite family of cases with two steps - a base and an inductive step. It is the shape of every loop invariant, every recurrence, and every claim that a training loop decreases.
days.recall: From memory: name the two steps of induction, in the right order.
days.misconception: Confusing mathematical induction with 'inductive' machine learning. One is a rule of proof; the other is fitting a pattern to data and hoping.
days.practice: Take the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n. Verify the closed form on the first fifty values in Python, then write the inductive step on paper. Both artefacts go in your log; the script alone is not the day.
days.check: State the induction hypothesis in one sentence and point at the exact line where you are allowed to assume it.
days.gate: Prove on paper, in four lines or fewer, that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared.

days.title: Recursive data types: the structure writes the code
days.idea: A type defined in terms of itself - a list is empty or a head plus a list, a tree is a leaf or a node plus trees - dictates the shape of the function: one case per constructor.
days.recall: From memory: how many clauses a function over a recursive type needs, and what each clause corresponds to.
days.misconception: Writing recursion from the inside out and forgetting the base case, then filing it as an infinite-loop bug instead of a missing clause.
days.practice: `../python-exercises/exercises/01_collections/06_flatten.py` - first count the constructors aloud, then write one clause for each.
days.check: Say which clause is the base case, and why the argument is guaranteed to get smaller every call.
days.gate: Sketch a nested data type of your own and its depth function without opening the page.

days.title: Sums and asymptotics: the price of an algorithm
days.idea: Big-O is a claim about growth, not about today's speed. Sums give the total work of a loop nest, and a constant that looks harmless is usually the size of your dataset.
days.recall: From memory: order these by growth - n log n, 2 to the n, n squared, log n, n.
days.misconception: Believing n squared means 'slow' on the laptop you actually have. A squared pass over thirty rows is free; a linear pass over thirty million is what will wake you up.
days.practice: Time two ways of answering 'have I seen this before?' - a list and a set - over 200,000 rows using `time.perf_counter`. Write down the ratio and which curve each followed.
days.check: Cold-write the summation for a double loop over n items and evaluate it to a closed form.
days.gate: Estimate, then measure, the complexity of your own Day 4 word-count exercise.

days.title: Probability spaces: what can happen, what you ask, what weighs
days.idea: Before any arithmetic, three objects must be named: the sample space, the event you are asking about, and the distribution that assigns mass. Monty Hall trips most people because the sample space was written down wrong.
days.recall: From memory: define sample space and event, then say which Monty Hall strategy wins and why.
days.misconception: Assuming the two remaining doors are equally likely after the host reveals one. The host's policy is part of the model, and changing it changes the answer.
days.practice: Simulate Monty Hall ten thousand times in standard-library Python for both strategies and print the two win rates. Predict the rates before you run it.
days.check: Write out the four outcomes of the game before you look at the simulation's output.
days.gate: State the sample space of your Day 8 CSV: every possible train-test split, and which event you are conditioning on when you compare them.

days.title: Conditional probability and Bayes: updating on evidence
days.idea: P(A given B) is a different quantity from P(B given A). Bayes' rule converts one into the other, which is precisely what a classifier does when it turns a likelihood into a posterior.
days.recall: From memory: write Bayes' rule as words before symbols, and say which piece a trained model hands you and which piece you actually wanted.
days.misconception: Base-rate neglect: believing a 99%-accurate test is conclusive for a condition one person in ten thousand has.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/04_responsible_ai/12_group_rates.py` - group rates are conditional probabilities. State which conditioning direction the file reports, and what the other direction would say.
days.check: Pick numbers you chose yourself, compute one base-rate example on paper, then check it in Python.
days.gate: Explain the difference between false-positive rate and positive predictive value to a Day 2 learner, using one example and no formulas.

days.title: Expectation: the value you should have before you roll
days.idea: Expectation is a weighted average over the sample space, and a loss function is an expectation - so a model fitted to the mean of your data is answering a question about the mean of your world.
days.recall: From memory: define expectation, and give the expectation of one fair die.
days.misconception: Confusing the expected value with the most likely value. They part company badly in skewed cases, and error distributions are skewed.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/03_regression_metrics.py` - mean absolute error and mean squared error are expectations of two different loss variables. Say which one punishes outliers harder, using the file's own numbers.
days.check: Write the sum that defines the expectation for your own six-outcome example.
days.gate: Explain why squared error is the expectation of a square rather than the square of an expectation.

days.title: Deviation: variance, standard deviation, and the trade you are about to meet
days.idea: Variance measures spread around the mean and standard deviation puts the units back. Two datasets with identical means can disagree completely once spread enters, which is why an error bar is a claim rather than a decoration.
days.recall: From memory: define variance, and say what squaring does to a large deviation compared with a small one.
days.misconception: Using raw errors as a spread measure. Positive and negative cancel, and the disagreement you were looking for disappears.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/02_standardize.py` - recompute mean, standard deviation and z-scores by hand first, then confirm the transformed column has mean zero and standard deviation one.
days.check: Cold-write the one-sentence idea of Days 9 to 16. This is the gate for the whole mathematics block; anything you cannot write goes back into your queue as its own day.
days.gate: Predict what one far-out point (1 part in 1000) does to a fitted line, then measure it. Name which metric you trusted and why.

days.title: What machine learning actually is
days.idea: Machine learning is a program whose behaviour is shaped by data instead of by hand-written rules; the test of it is performance on unseen examples.
days.recall: From memory, define machine learning in one sentence and give one example where you would NOT use it. If you cannot say the sentence, this day is a repeat day, not a reading day.
days.misconception: Believing a model is intelligent because it produced an output. An output is a prediction, not a truth.
days.practice: Open `../ml-exercises/README.md` and read the pathway list only. Then write, in your log, which of the 12 local exercises maps to each idea you expect to meet in this course. No code today.
days.check: Say the definition out loud without the page open, then write one sentence on why unseen data matters. Both must exist in your log before marking complete.
days.gate: Explain the difference between a rule-based program and a learned program using a non-tech example of your own.

days.title: Supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement: the categories
days.idea: The three families differ by what the learning signal is: labelled answers, unlabelled structure, or reward after acting.
days.misconception: Calling anything 'AI' that is only if-else logic. Name the learning signal or it is not a category.
days.practice: Take three apps you use daily (M-Pesa alerts, YouTube, SMS) and classify the learning signal in each. Write it down; this is the skill the recall blocks will re-test.
days.check: Re-test Day 18 from memory before reading. If it faded, redo Day 18's gate first.
days.gate: Give one worked example per category without looking, and say what the model would be wrong about in each.

days.title: The ML toolbox: models as tools, not identities
days.idea: A toolbox of model families (regression, trees, clustering, nets) chosen by the shape of data and the decision needed.
days.practice: Do `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` (stdlib, offline). The point is train/test separation before any model exists.
days.check: Run `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and read every line it prints, pass or fail.
days.gate: Pick a tool for a problem you define yourself, and defend the pick against one alternative.

days.title: Data scrubbing and setting up your data
days.idea: Most of the work is making the data trustworthy: missing values, duplicates, wrong units, leakage.
days.misconception: Cleaning after fitting. Anything computed from the whole dataset before the split leaks the test set into training.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/02_standardize.py`. Then deliberately corrupt one row and re-run to watch the failure.
days.check: Day 20 recall (1 back) plus: name three leakage routes you have personally caused.
days.gate: Clean a small messy CSV of your own and record each choice with a reason.

days.title: Data engineering, the way production does it
days.idea: Training data is a pipeline with owners, schemas and versions, not a folder of files.
days.practice: Sketch a data pipeline for one SyncSenta-style dataset on paper: source, transform, store, validate, serve. Mark where it breaks.
days.check: Compare your sketch against the extracted text and name one stage you invented that the author warns about.
days.gate: Explain schema drift to a non-engineer in three sentences.

days.title: Regression analysis: fitting a line you can defend
days.idea: Regression estimates a relationship; the fit quality is a claim about data, not a promise about the world.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/04_fit_line.py` then `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/03_regression_metrics.py`.
days.check: Day 22 recall (1 back) and Day 19 recall (3 back).
days.gate: Report one metric in your own words, then say what it hides.

days.title: Error metrics and validation sets that mean something
days.idea: MAE, MSE and hold-out validation answer different questions; choose the metric from the cost of being wrong.
days.misconception: Chasing accuracy on an imbalanced problem. 99% accuracy can be a useless model.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py`. Predict the numbers before running, then compare.
days.check: Day 23 recall (1 back), Day 21 (3 back), Day 18 (back to the definition).
days.gate: For a loan-approval problem, name the metric you would defend in a review and why.

days.title: Bias and variance — plus a hard review of Days 18–24
days.idea: Underfitting misses structure; overfitting memorises noise. Complexity trades one error for the other.
days.practice: No new exercise. Re-solve `01_split_data.py` and `03_regression_metrics.py` from a blank file, closed solutions. Log every mistake.
days.check: Write the one-sentence idea of Days 18–24 from memory first; only then open the pages. Faded days get re-added to your queue.
days.gate: 90% of the recall prompts answered cold. If not, repeat this day tomorrow instead of advancing.

days.title: Decision trees and ensemble modelling
days.idea: Trees split on features to make decisions explainable; bagging and boosting buy accuracy by averaging or correcting many trees.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/02_unsupervised/07_assign_centroid.py` is adjacent practice in nearest-neighbour thinking; then hand-draw a tree for a daily decision.
days.check: Day 25 (1 back), Day 23 (3 back), Day 19 (7 back).
days.gate: Explain why many weak learners beat one strong learner, with an analogy you would use with a student.

days.title: Artificial neural networks without the mysticism
days.idea: A network is weighted arithmetic plus a non-linearity, tuned by gradient descent; layers compose features.
days.misconception: Thinking depth alone equals understanding. Depth is capacity, not comprehension.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/06_gradient_step.py`. Predict the next weight before running.
days.check: Day 26 (1 back), Day 24 (3 back), Day 20 (7 back).
days.gate: Walk one gradient step by hand on paper with numbers you choose.

days.title: Logistic regression, properly (interview depth)
days.idea: Logistic regression is a linear score squashed into a probability; the decision threshold is a business choice.
days.practice: Re-derive the sigmoid from the page without looking, then code it in the style of `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py`.
days.check: Day 27 (1 back), Day 25 (3 back), Day 21 (7 back).
days.gate: Answer two interview questions from this chapter in writing, closed book.

days.title: Information theory: entropy as surprise
days.idea: Entropy measures average surprise; cross-entropy is the loss you pay when your predicted distribution differs from reality.
days.practice: Compute entropy by hand for a two-outcome event at p=0.5, 0.9, 0.1. Then compute it in Python from scratch, no libraries.
days.check: Day 28 (1 back), Day 26 (3 back), Day 22 (7 back).
days.gate: Explain why cross-entropy punishes confident wrong answers harder than loss functions you already know.

days.title: How large language models actually work
days.idea: An LLM predicts the next token from context; training is expensive, inference is a search over probabilities.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/09_chunk_text.py`. Everything here is local strings, no API calls.
days.check: Day 29 (1 back), Day 27 (3 back), Day 23 (7 back), Day 18 (21 back — the definition again).
days.gate: Explain a hallucination using only next-token prediction, no hand-waving.

days.title: Retrieval: chunking, embedding, ranking
days.idea: Retrieval grounds generation in documents you chose; chunk quality and ranking decide what the model gets to see.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/10_rank_documents.py` plus `08_cosine_similarity.py`.
days.check: Day 30 (1 back), Day 28 (3 back), Day 24 (7 back), Day 19 (21 back).
days.gate: Given a wrong answer from a RAG setup, list the three places the fault could live.

days.title: Why machine learning systems fail
days.idea: Failures are usually pipeline, data and feedback-loop failures, not model-quality failures.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/04_responsible_ai/12_group_rates.py`. Note which group metric moves and why that matters.
days.check: Day 31 (1 back), Day 29 (3 back), Day 25 (7 back — review day again), Day 20 (21 back).
days.gate: Write a one-page post-mortem for a system that got silently worse, naming the monitoring you would have needed.

days.title: Build and optimise one model end to end
days.idea: You own the whole loop now: split, clean, fit, measure, explain, improve.
days.practice: Write a single stdlib Python program that loads a small CSV you choose, splits it, fits the line from Day 23, and reports metrics from Day 24. No pandas. Then re-run `../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and keep it green.
days.check: Cold-write the one-sentence idea of Days 18–32. Anything you cannot write goes back into your queue as its own day.
days.gate: Present the model in five minutes to an imaginary colleague, including one thing you would change with more data.

days.title: The landscape again, this time in a practitioner's words
days.idea: Geron's opening moves the question from 'what is learning' to 'what is the task, what is the signal, what is the model'. Every project starts by naming those three, not by choosing a library.
days.recall: From memory, one sentence each: the Day 18 definition of machine learning, the Day 19 categories, and the Day 20 line about models being tools.
days.misconception: Believing a state-of-the-art model can rescue a task that was never specified. It cannot, and the benchmark will not tell you that you skipped it.
days.practice: Take any one file from `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/` and write its task, signal and model as three labelled lines before you touch the code.
days.check: State what the training signal is for each supervised family you met on Day 19, from memory.
days.gate: Explain to your Day 18 self why the model is the last of the three things you choose.

days.title: End to end, with real data and a numbered frame
days.idea: The project method is a sequence you can be taken to task for skipping: frame the problem, choose the measure, get the data, look at it, prepare it, fit, tune, present - and then automate the whole pipeline so the next run is a command.
days.recall: From memory: name the project steps in order, and say which two must happen before you download anything.
days.misconception: Starting with the model because downloading data is boring. The boring step is where projects are won, and it is the one people re-do under deadline.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` then `02_standardize.py` - write the frame and the metric sentence for one dataset you chose, and write the metric before the split, not after.
days.check: Produce the metric sentence ('we measure X on Y in order to Z') before any code runs, and keep it in the log.
days.gate: Show the five numbers you would take to a first project review, without opening your notes.

days.title: Classification: the confusion matrix is the deliverable
days.idea: Classifiers are judged by a matrix, not by an accuracy. Which errors you can afford decides the metric, and the decision threshold is a business choice you can move without retraining anything.
days.recall: From memory: draw the two-by-two confusion matrix and write precision and recall out of it.
days.misconception: Reporting accuracy on a problem with one positive in a hundred, then being surprised that a constant 'no' scores 99%.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py` - compute true/false positives and negatives, then precision, recall and F1 on deliberately imbalanced data you build yourself.
days.check: Name which cell of the matrix your most recent real project actually looked at, and which one it ignored.
days.gate: Set a threshold for a screening test given a cost per false alarm, and defend the trade in one sentence.

days.title: Training models: a loss surface, and walking downhill on it
days.idea: Every trainable model is parameters plus a loss, and training is a search downhill on that loss - so the learning rate, the shape of the surface, and the scale of your features decide whether you arrive or oscillate in place.
days.recall: From memory: in one clause each, what happens when the learning rate is too large and when it is too small.
days.misconception: Treating gradient descent as a fact about the model instead of a search. A perfect model class can still fail to train, and unscaled features are the usual reason.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/06_gradient_step.py` - do one step on paper first, then verify the code's numbers match your arithmetic digit for digit.
days.check: Write the update rule from memory and label every symbol in it.
days.gate: Explain why the scaling you did on Day 17 changes the shape of the surface and not the optimum.

days.title: Ensembles: many weak, decorrelated guesses beat one strong one
days.idea: Averaging independent errors shrinks variance. Random forests buy that decorrelation by resampling rows and features, and bagging works even when each individual tree is deliberately kept weak.
days.recall: From memory: say why averaging helps, and name the two randomisations a random forest uses.
days.misconception: Ensembling twenty copies of the same badly-specified model. Averaging removes variance; it does not average bias away.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/04_fit_line.py` - fit three lines on three bootstrap samples of the same data, average their predictions, and report each single error against the ensemble's.
days.check: Cold-write the bias-variance sentence from Day 25 in your own words.
days.gate: Predict which degrades first when you double the ensemble size - bias or variance - then measure it and say whether you were right.

days.title: Why nobody agrees on what AGI means
days.idea: AGI is a contested term, not a milestone. Togelius opens by saying the definitions conflict; the useful move is to ask general at *what*, and to treat intelligence as a measured capacity to do many tasks rather than a substance a system either has or lacks.
days.recall: Day 33 (1 back), Day 31 (3 back), Day 27 (7 back). From memory: name one thing your Day 27 neural network cannot do that a Day 31 retrieval system can, and say which of the two is more general.
days.misconception: Treating AGI as a finish line a lab crosses on a Tuesday. A single threshold cannot be measured across tasks of different difficulty, so any claim of we reached AGI is a claim about the benchmark, not the machine.
days.practice: Open `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` and its solution. Everything you say about generality must be tested on data the model has not seen - that is the whole reason the train/test split exists. Then write the sentence: my generality claim will be tested on ___.
days.check: Say the definition of AGI the book works with, without the page, and give one example where that definition would classify a spreadsheet as intelligent.
days.gate: Explain to a friend why passing the test is weak evidence of generality, using a test you have personally taken.

days.title: A brief history of superhuman narrow machines
days.idea: Machines have beaten humans at one celebrated skill after another - checkers, chess, Go, image recognition, quiz games - and each win turned out to be narrow. The pattern is that every milestone quietly needed more human-built scaffolding than the publicity admitted.
days.recall: Day 39 (1 back), Day 32 (3 back), Day 28 (7 back). Name three superhuman narrow systems and, for each, the one human decision that made its victory possible.
days.misconception: Believing a win at a game proves general ability. It proves the machine can search a well-defined state space with a hand-written evaluation function, which is a different claim entirely.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py` - implement it, then look at what the exercise makes you count. Write one paragraph: what would Deep Blue's confusion matrix look like, and what would it have no rows for?
days.check: Say why a benchmark can be saturated by narrow methods, and name the benchmark your own field treats as if it were generality.
days.gate: Given a system that beats every human at task T, list three things it still cannot do, and say which of the three a recruiter would care about.

days.title: Intelligence (natural): the measurement before the machine
days.idea: Human intelligence was made scientific by psychometrics: many cognitive tests correlate, and that correlation - the g factor - is a statistical observation, not a discovered organ. AGI debates inherit this measurement problem wholesale.
days.recall: Day 40 (1 back), Day 33 (3 back), Day 29 (7 back). Define the g factor in one sentence and say what it is a correlation between.
days.misconception: Reifying the score. IQ names a pattern in test results; treating it as a fixed quantity inside a head is the error, and the same error waits for anyone who reduces a model to one benchmark number.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/10_rank_documents.py` then `11_parse_model_json.py` - both are about ranking and scoring outputs. Run them, then write the sentence a score ranks, it does not explain, and name one place in this course where you have been tempted to forget it.
days.check: Explain in one sentence why factor analysis finds structure in data rather than in people.
days.gate: Argue both sides for ninety seconds each: g is real, and g is an artefact of how the tests are built. Then say which side a measurement designer should assume.

days.title: Intelligence (artificial): how to score a machine fairly
days.idea: If intelligence is measured performance across many task environments, the hard part is the task distribution: normalise by difficulty, weight breadth over peak, and refuse to average a chess engine with a spam filter.
days.recall: Day 41 (1 back), Day 39 (3 back), Day 30 (7 back). State the definition of artificial intelligence this book measures against, then name the two things it forces you to specify.
days.misconception: Comparing systems on one task and calling the winner more intelligent. That is a claim about the task; a fair comparison says what fraction of the task space was covered.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/03_regression_metrics.py` is the seed of this day. Reuse its idea: write a rubric that scores three different tiny programs on breadth, not only accuracy. Write the rubric before you pick the programs.
days.check: Say how you would normalise two benchmarks of different difficulty, out loud, without notes.
days.gate: Design a 10-task test that would separate a calculator from a language model, and say which of your ten tasks is doing the most work.

days.title: Varieties of AGI: the taxonomy that ends most arguments
days.idea: AGI collapses several independent properties: breadth, robustness, autonomy, and generality of learning. Once you separate the axes you can stop arguing about the label - a system can be strong on one axis and absent on another, which is why two people can both be right about the same model.
days.recall: Day 42 (1 back), Day 41 (3 back), Day 31 (7 back). Name the axes the taxonomy separates, then place one system you used this month on each.
days.misconception: Reading AGI as one dial from weak to strong. It is a set of dials, and marketing flattens them on purpose because a single dial makes a better headline.
days.practice: Score four systems you already have on this laptop - the models from `../ml-exercises/`, a retrieval pipeline, a code agent, and a spreadsheet macro - on breadth, robustness and autonomy, 1 to 5, in your log. That table is the deliverable.
days.check: Say which axis your own work genuinely improves, and which one you have been implying it improves.
days.gate: Someone says this model is nearly AGI. Ask the two questions that make the sentence precise, then answer them for a system of your choice.

days.title: Practical AGI development: what you would build this week
days.idea: Building toward generality now means engineering transfer between tasks: shared representations, world models that predict, and architectures where learning one thing does not erase another. It is a programme of components, not one magic algorithm.
days.recall: Day 43 (1 back), Day 42 (3 back), Day 32 (7 back). Name the three component families and say which one Day 22's data-debt discussion already told you how to fail at.
days.misconception: Believing scale alone delivers the components. More compute buys the same behaviour faster; it does not buy a world model and it does not protect an old skill from being overwritten.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/02_unsupervised/08_cosine_similarity.py` - shared representations are this day's claim made concrete. Implement it, then compare the vectors of two tasks you care about and write down what similar would actually mean for transfer between them.
days.check: Explain catastrophic forgetting in one sentence and say which of your own pipelines is most exposed to it.
days.gate: Sketch, in six lines, the smallest system that learns task B without losing task A. Name the part that would actually break.

days.title: Self-supervised learning of foundation models
days.idea: Foundation models work because prediction without labels is nearly free: mask a span, predict it, and the gradient arrives from the corpus itself. That is the bridge from the supervised world of Day 23 to the LLM world of Days 30-31, and it explains both the reach and the brittleness.
days.recall: Day 44 (1 back), Day 43 (3 back), Day 30 (9 back - it is the LLM day). Say what the label is in self-supervised learning and where it comes from.
days.misconception: Thinking self-supervised means unsupervised in the Day 24 clustering sense. There is still a target and still a loss; the trick is that the target is generated from the input instead of by an annotator.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/09_chunk_text.py` then `11_parse_model_json.py`. Chunk a document, then predict what a masked model would have to infer about your own writing. Record the one chunk boundary that changed meaning.
days.check: Explain next-token prediction versus masking, and say which one makes retrieval augmentation necessary.
days.gate: A stakeholder says we will fine-tune our own foundation model. List the three questions that decide whether that is reasonable, and the answer that would stop you.

days.title: Open-ended learning in virtual worlds
days.idea: Games and simulated worlds let a system be tested on tasks nobody wrote for it: co-evolve an agent with its environment and you get a curriculum that never runs out. Quality-diversity beats a single best score, because the interesting result is a range of working strategies.
days.recall: Day 45 (1 back), Day 44 (3 back), Day 33 (8 back). Define quality-diversity in one sentence and contrast it with the single-number ranking you wrote about on Day 41.
days.misconception: Assuming simulated results transfer. A world model built by a game engine still differs from the messy physical and social world, and the gap is exactly where the failures land.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/06_gradient_step.py` is the smallest possible agent learning from feedback. Run it, then write the local version of this day's idea: a fitness function plus one thing that must vary, not merely improve.
days.check: Say why an environment that cannot get harder teaches nothing, and name the exercise in this course whose difficulty is fixed by its test suite.
days.gate: Design an open-ended curriculum for a skill you are learning that is not coding. Name the agent, the environment, and what counts as a novel task.

days.title: Consciousness, superintelligence, and what any of it owes you
days.idea: Three separate questions get fused in public debate: whether a machine is conscious (untestable, with no agreed theory), whether it will be much better than us at everything (a distribution claim, not a switch), and who governs the consequences (an institutional claim). Mixing them produces confident nonsense in both directions.
days.recall: Day 46 (1 back), Day 45 (3 back), Day 40 (7 back). Separate the three questions in one sentence each, without the page.
days.misconception: Reasoning about machine suffering or machine supremacy from human intuition, which was built for other humans and for tools, and is unreliable for both of these.
days.practice: Write the paragraph you would actually send a decision-maker: what is genuinely uncertain about AGI, what is merely contested, and what is already decided by systems you have run. Then read `../security-exercises/exercises/03_response/08_incident_checklist.py` and steal its discipline - name the owner and the trigger, not the mood.
days.check: Name one AGI claim you have repeated that you cannot now support, and say what evidence would change your mind.
days.gate: Argue the cautious position and the dismissive position for two minutes each, then say which one you would bet your work on and why.

days.title: Cognitive architectures: the survey that predates the hype
days.idea: Before foundation models, people built whole minds on paper and in code - SOAR, ACT-R, Cyc and the rest - by deciding what memory is, what a goal is, and how a decision gets made. The value of the survey is vocabulary: architecture is what you choose when the model is not enough.
days.recall: Day 47 (1 back), Day 46 (3 back), Day 44 (4 back), Day 41 (7 back). Name two architectures from the survey and the one thing each insists a mind must have.
days.misconception: Assuming the field started with transformers. Working memory, an episodic store, planning over a world model - all of it was engineered and argued about decades ago, badly, on the record.
days.practice: Take the three component families you listed on Day 44 and match each to a named mechanism in this chapter. Where the chapter's mechanism is stronger than your plan, change your plan and log the change.
days.check: Say what a cognitive architecture provides that a model checkpoint does not.
days.gate: Explain to your Day 18 self why a chatbot plus memory is still not an architecture, and name the missing piece by its old name.

days.title: From prompts to context: engineering what the agent is shown
days.idea: Context engineering is deciding what an agent sees and when: the semantic blueprint, the chaining of steps, the validation loop. It replaces write a cleverer prompt with design the information flow, which is why it behaves like software engineering and not like magic.
days.recall: Day 48 (1 back), Day 47 (3 back), Day 45 (4 back), Day 42 (7 back). Define context in one sentence, then say what Day 45's token-prediction limit has to do with it.
days.misconception: Believing a bigger context window removes the problem. More room to put things is not a plan for what belongs there, and a full window degrades quietly rather than failing loudly.
days.practice: Build the smallest real version: take one unsolved exercise from `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/` and write a context file an agent would need to solve it - task, allowed tools, two worked examples, and the validation check. Then attempt it yourself using only that file and log what you had left out.
days.check: Name the three parts of your context file the agent could not have inferred, and the one it could.
days.gate: Debug this: the agent answers well on the sample and badly in production. Give the three context-related causes you would rule out first, in order, and say which is most likely.

days.title: Agentic coding: a teammate who still needs review
days.idea: Agentic coding means delegating a task, not a keystroke: the system decomposes it, touches the environment, and produces work that must be reviewed like any other contribution. The skill moves to specification, review and rollback - the parts an agent cannot own.
days.recall: Day 49 (1 back), Day 48 (3 back), Day 46 (4 back), Day 43 (7 back). Say what an agent may decide and what stays yours, as two lists.
days.misconception: Believing autonomy removes review, or that a passing test suite proves good design. Agents optimise for the check you wrote, and a weak check is worse than none because it feels like safety.
days.practice: No service needed: pick one exercise from `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/` you have not solved, write its specification as if handing it to a teammate (constraints, tests, forbidden changes), then solve it yourself and diff your thinking against the spec. The gap is the review skill you just practised.
days.check: Name three things you will never delegate on this laptop, and why each is cheap for you and expensive for an agent.
days.gate: Write the two-sentence policy you would give a team adopting agentic coding tomorrow, including who is accountable when it breaks production.

days.title: Trust and governance as architecture: the closing gate
days.idea: Governance is not a document bolted on after deployment; it is a property of the design - who can act, what is provable, what gets logged, and what happens when the operator is wrong. This short paper argues the architecture has to carry the trust the humans will not grant.
days.recall: Day 50 (1 back), Day 49 (3 back), Day 47 (4 back), Day 44 (7 back), Day 25 (21 back). From memory: name the one component you would refuse to ship without an audit trail.
days.misconception: Treating governance as compliance theatre. If nothing changes when a control is violated, it is a policy paragraph, not an architectural property.
days.practice: Write the capstone page: (a) the system you would build with what you have now, (b) the three failure modes from Days 43, 47 and 50 that apply to it, (c) the architectural control that answers each, and (d) the evidence a stranger could check. Then run `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and `python3 ../security-exercises/run_tests.py` and log both outputs - finishing the course means the code you wrote still passes.
days.check: Say, without notes, the difference between a control and a policy. Your page must contain at least two of the former.
days.gate: Defend the capstone to three critics in turn: a Day 18 beginner, a Day 43 taxonomist, and a regulator. Where you cannot answer, that is next week's study, not this course's gap.

days.title: Specifying what agents owe each other
days.idea: Before agent frameworks were a product category, this 1998 workshop paper was already formalising what it means for two programs to communicate rather than merely exchange bytes: the specification is about the knowledge and commitments that change when a speech act is performed, not about the message format. Read it as the ancestor of every tool call you have written.
days.recall: From memory: the Day 51 difference between a control and a policy - then say which of the two a speech act is.
days.misconception: Treating a speech act as a message. The act is the change it licenses: after a promise the agent owes an outcome, and the specification has to say what happens when it does not deliver.
days.check: Without notes, write the three things that must be true of agent B after A asks it to do something, and say which of the three your own scripts ever check.
days.gate: Take one automation from `~/Desktop/ML/codes/` and specify it in this vocabulary: who knows what, who is committed to what, what the log must show. If you cannot state a commitment that could be violated, you have a script, not an agent.
days.practice: Write `~/Desktop/ML/codes/spec_agents.py`: two functions, requester and executor, that exchange a dict and refuse to advance state unless the act is one of `ask`, `promise`, `notify`. Make an illegal act raise. Then run `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and log the output so you know the existing exercises still pass.

days.title: Reactive cooperation: getting along without a plan
days.idea: The next paper in the same volume argues the opposite instinct: cooperation need not be planned or negotiated, it can be a property of how agents' behaviours are coupled, each making the other's next move legible. Hold both papers together - formal specification versus emergent coordination is still today's argument.
days.recall: From memory: Day 52's three post-act conditions, and one thing each of them assumes about the other agent.
days.misconception: 'Reactive' does not mean mindless and it does not mean goal-less. It means the coordination work is done by the environment and the coupling rather than by an internal model of the partner.
days.check: In one sentence each: what Day 52's agents must represent, and what Day 53's agents can get away with not representing.
days.gate: Find one place where your Day 52 script would be simpler as reactive coupling, and one place where it would be unsafe. Defend both.
days.practice: Add a `--reactive` mode to `spec_agents.py` in which the executor never receives a message: it watches a shared state file and acts when a field changes. Run both modes on the same job and diff the outputs. `python3 ../python-exercises/run_tests.py` still has to pass.

days.title: Why self-improvement overfits its own measuring rig
days.idea: The paper's own claim list: recursive self-improvement overfits the harness that scores it, so gains on the evolve split do not transfer out of distribution. Read the fix as experimental design, not AI theory - freeze what you optimise against, keep a genuinely untouched split, and re-test with a weaker backbone that never took part in the search.
days.recall: From memory: Days 52 and 53's two kinds of cooperation, and what the difference costs in trust.
days.misconception: Confusing 'the agent got better' with 'the agent got better at the thing we were scoring'. Overfitting to a harness is invisible from inside that harness.
days.check: Name the three splits in the paper's design and say which one is allowed to influence the search.
days.gate: Point at one thing you optimised this month - a prompt, a study routine, a script - and state how you would know it was overfit to your own measuring procedure rather than actually better.
days.practice: Write the paper's evaluation structure as a checklist for your own work in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/curriculum/rsi-eval-checklist.md`, following the house style of the `curriculum/README.md` already in that folder. Then re-read your Day 32 notes on why machine learning systems fail and mark which checklist item catches which failure.

days.title: Attribution: the capability a wargame exposed
days.idea: Key takeaways from a RAND exercise run on the Robot Insurgency scenario, in which the United States takes a massive cyberattack from rogue AI agents. Proper attribution emerged as the binding problem - you cannot respond to what you cannot pin on an actor - and the exercises were structured to surface that before the technical response. Governance pressure arriving from the security side, after Day 51.
days.recall: From memory: the Day 54 overfitting result in one sentence, and the Day 51 architectural control you said you would not ship without.
days.misconception: Reading this as prediction. A wargame's value is not that it foresees the attack but that it shows which capability is missing when the attack is weird.
days.check: Name the two capabilities the exercises found weakest, and say which gap is technical and which is organisational.
days.gate: Run your Days 52-53 two-agent script as a wargame: invent one scenario it handles badly, write the scenario down, and say whether the fix is code, specification, or procedure.
days.practice: `python3 ../security-exercises/run_tests.py`, then read every filename in `../security-exercises/exercises/` and write at the top of your log which one is closest to the attribution problem in this report, and why.

days.title: Trained, not programmed: the dataset is a design decision
days.idea: The book's AI-in-a-nutshell passage: machine learning is the part of AI that is not programmed but trained - the system is adjusted against a dataset until the desired behaviour is as good as it can get - which makes the dataset a design decision rather than a precondition.
days.recall: From memory: Day 55's two weakest capabilities, and Day 18's own definition of machine learning in your words.
days.misconception: 'We used AI' as a description. If you cannot say what the model was trained on and what it would have done differently on a different sample, the sentence carries no information.
days.check: Define training, dataset and model in one sentence each, using the author's words rather than yours.
days.gate: Take one tool you use daily and say whether the behaviour you rely on is trained, hardcoded, or configured - and how you would find out.
days.practice: Open `~/Desktop/ML/codes/mean.py` and `mssing_data_filler_mean.py`, the two scripts you have already written, and put one paragraph above each explaining what the data has to look like for the code to be correct. Then `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py`.

days.title: ELIZA, 1966: the reader does half the work
days.idea: A pattern-matching script that people experienced as a listener. The book uses it to make the point that the impression of understanding is produced as much by the reader as by the system - the oldest version of the failure you have been reading about all week.
days.recall: From memory: Day 56's definition of training, and the one thing a 1966 script has that a modern chatbot has lost.
days.misconception: That ELIZA was a crude program we have outgrown. The failure it demonstrates is still the current failure: fluency is read as competence.
days.check: Say why a twenty-line pattern matcher was convincing, and what that implies for a system that genuinely is not a pattern matcher.
days.gate: Run the ELIZA you wrote and record the exact moment you started cooperating with it - the line where you supplied meaning it had not produced.
days.practice: Write `~/Desktop/ML/codes/eliza.py`: three rewrite rules, one keyword list, a loop that never breaks character. Keep it under 25 lines, run it on yourself, and then attempt `../prompt-exercises/01.md` exercise one with the same discipline - specify only what you want done, not who you are.

days.title: Where frontier capability actually comes from
days.idea: The economics page: training compute is now the dominant cost, and a few hundred people with more than eleven billion dollars across four funding rounds outperform organisations with thousands of research scientists. Read it as a claim about the source of capability, and hold it against Day 54 - an expensive model can still be wrong about its own gains.
days.recall: From memory: Day 57's lesson about fluency, and the two resources the page says constrain frontier models.
days.misconception: That capability tracks the number of researchers, or that a large budget is evidence of understanding.
days.check: State the two constraining resources, and name one thing money in that list cannot buy.
days.gate: Argue against the page you just read in three sentences, then say which part of your rebuttal is a factual claim and which is a value claim.
days.practice: Read `~/Desktop/ML/codes/curriculum/01-python-foundations.md` and mark every place the guide assumes access you do not have on this machine. For each, write one line on the local alternative - which is your real constraint, and the one no budget solves.

days.title: Humanoid robots: a forecast to be priced, not believed
days.idea: The convergence chapter, where the book turns to humanoid embodiments as the fusion of form and intellect - the same models that talk now planning bodies. Treat the argument as a forecast with a cost of being wrong, which is how Day 55's wargame read it and how Day 54 read a benchmark.
days.recall: From memory: Day 58's two resources, and the limitation Day 32 said most failures come from.
days.misconception: That embodiment is the last mile. The hard parts - perception under distribution shift, recovery from an unsafe action - are the same parts the papers on Days 54 and 55 call unsolved.
days.check: Name the one capability the book says is nearly ready and the one it quietly assumes.
days.gate: Write the forecast's failure mode as a specification sentence: 'this system is unsafe when ___ and nothing in the design detects it.'
days.practice: `python3 ../iot-exercises/exercises/01_validate_sensor.py`, then break the input deliberately: a sensor reporting a constant, then one reporting 9999. Record what the validation catches and what it lets through. That gap is the humanoid problem at toy scale.

days.title: Short beats long: 21 words of instruction
days.idea: A practitioner's counterweight to the theory chapters. In Google Workspace use, the most effective prompts averaged about 21 words; the guidance is to specify task, audience and format rather than to add length or persona. It is measurement from inside a product, so read it alongside Day 54's warning about measuring your own gains.
days.recall: From memory: Day 59's assumed capability, and the one sentence you would keep from Day 56's definition.
days.misconception: That a better prompt is a longer prompt. The chapter's own data says the effective ones are short and specific; most of the extra length describes the asker rather than the ask.
days.check: Rewrite one of your own long prompts to under 25 words without losing the task, the audience or the format.
days.gate: Show the before/after pair on a real piece of your own writing and say which version you would put in front of a client.
days.practice: Work through `../prompt-exercises/01.md`: do the first three exercises twice, once in your usual style and once under 25 words. Record which version produced the answer you actually used, and keep both.

days.title: Prompt chains: the format is the interface
days.idea: The integration chapter: prompts arranged as a customer-service workflow - standardising communications, then improving them, then enabling self-service - where the value sits in the sequence and the shared context rather than in any single prompt.
days.recall: From memory: Day 60's 21-word finding and the three things a short prompt must still specify.
days.misconception: Collecting prompts. A library of unrelated good prompts is a list; a workflow is prompts whose outputs are each other's inputs, with a format both sides honour.
days.check: Name the output format that makes two of this chapter's prompts compose.
days.gate: Design a three-prompt chain for something you actually do weekly, and say at which link a wrong answer would be invisible.
days.practice: Write that chain into `../prompt-exercises/02_chain.md`, then run the first link for real and check whether its output is usable as the second link's input without editing. Log the result honestly - 'no, not yet' is a pass for this day.

days.title: Seventy years of believing the last obstacle was the final one
days.idea: The history chapter from a builder's book: funding growths and lapses, symbolists against connectionists, and the recurring conviction that the current blocker was incidental. Useful as calibration in both directions - it is the best argument available for and against Day 59's convergence claims.
days.recall: From memory: Day 61's distinction between a list and a workflow, and Day 40's superhuman narrow machines.
days.misconception: That the history is a straight line to now. It is a series of resets, each caused by a limit the field had treated as incidental.
days.check: Name two AI winters and the specific limitation that triggered each.
days.gate: Say which limitation today's models treat as incidental, and which of the two winters your answer resembles.
days.practice: Write a one-page timeline in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/curriculum/ai-timeline.md`: exactly six entries, one line each on what broke. Six rather than ten - the exercise is selection, and you will have to argue with yourself to make it.

days.title: Your first network: the code is short, the judgement is not
days.idea: The book moves from basics to a trained artificial neural network in a few pages, and the lesson is proportion: the model itself is small, while the work is in shaping the data, choosing layers, and reading the loss curve.
days.recall: From memory: Day 27's demystified network, and the three stages of Day 21's data set-up.
days.misconception: That a network which trains is a network which works. Loss going down is enough to feel productive and proves almost nothing about deployed behaviour.
days.check: Say what the loss curve tells you about this model and what it does not.
days.gate: Change one hyper-parameter in your own run, predict the effect before running it, then explain the gap between prediction and result.
days.practice: Build the smallest network you can on data you already have, starting from `~/Desktop/ML/codes/frame.py` and `data_visualization.py`. Under 40 lines. If no deep-learning library is installed on this machine, write the forward pass and a gradient step by hand - it is the better exercise and needs nothing downloaded. Then `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py`.

days.title: Convolution: structure imposed instead of learned
days.idea: Convolutional networks as feedforward networks with local receptive fields and shared weights - vision-first architecture, later borrowed by language for unstructured input. The teaching point is the trade: structure bought with fewer parameters costs flexibility.
days.recall: From memory: Day 63's split between training and working, and Day 27's layers.
days.misconception: That a CNN 'knows' objects. It knows patterns that survive the pooling hierarchy, which is exactly why a change of texture defeats it.
days.check: In one sentence: what parameter sharing buys, and what it costs.
days.gate: Give one input a CNN would classify confidently and wrongly, and say what your answer assumes about its training set.
days.practice: `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py`, then read the folder names under `../ml-exercises/exercises/` and pick the one closest to image or grid structure. Attempt it without opening `solutions/`, and log the failure before you look at the answer.

days.title: Recurrence: making time an input
days.idea: Recurrent networks accept sequences by carrying state between steps, which is what lets a network treat time as data. Read this as the thing Transformers displaced, so you can say precisely what was displaced - fixed-length input was not the only difference.
days.recall: From memory: Day 64's structure-for-flexibility trade, and Day 30's description of how a language model steps.
days.misconception: That recurrence is memory in the useful sense. Untreated it is memory that decays, and most engineering between 1990 and 2017 exists to stop the decay.
days.check: Say why a vanilla RNN forgets, and name the mechanism a gate provides instead.
days.gate: Explain to a Day 18 beginner why an RNN can take an input of any length and a feedforward network cannot.
days.practice: Write a character-level predictor in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/rnn_toy.py` on a text file you own: keep a hidden vector, update it per character, predict the next one. No framework. Accuracy is not the point - feeling the state is. Log what you think you would have to change to preserve structure over long distances.

days.title: Reinforcement learning and the reward you cannot game
days.idea: Reinforcement learning as the book presents it: agents that perceive and react, learning from reward rather than labelled examples, which moves the difficulty to credit assignment - deciding which action deserved the outcome.
days.recall: From memory: Day 65's decay problem, and Day 19's three categories in one line each.
days.misconception: That reward is the easy part. Designing a reward signal that cannot be gamed is Day 54's harness-overfitting problem relocated from evaluation into training.
days.check: State the credit-assignment problem in one sentence and give one example of reward hacking.
days.gate: Design a reward for your own study routine on this course that you could not cheat, and say honestly how long it would survive.
days.practice: Read `../metta-exercises/README.md` and `../wolfram-exercises/README.md` - both are scaffolds whose exercises are not written yet. Pick one and write the first exercise yourself: a grid world where you must name the state before acting. Save it as `01_grid.py` in that folder and run it.

days.title: Deployment: the model acquires a service history
days.idea: The book's last mile: writing the application is only a small portion of what it takes, because a model in production needs monitoring, drift detection and retraining - it has become a component with a history rather than an artefact with a version.
days.recall: From memory: Day 63's loss-curve limits, Day 66's ungammable reward, and Day 51's control-versus-policy.
days.misconception: That deployment ends the engineering. A model with no monitored input distribution is a bug that fires slowly.
days.check: Name three things you must log from day one that you would never think of while building.
days.gate: Write the maintenance plan for the smallest thing you have actually run more than twice - one paragraph per item, including who reads the log and what they do when it warns.
days.practice: Take `~/Desktop/ML/codes/jup.py` or any script you genuinely run and add three lines of honesty: a schema check on its input, one warning when the input deviates, and a timestamped log line. Then `python3 ../python-exercises/run_tests.py`.

days.title: What has to be true for a machine to be intelligent
days.idea: The definition arrived at from the device's point of view: a machine must know what to do with the information it receives, and that knowledge may be hardcoded rules, like the early expert systems, or learned parameters. It is Day 56's point made by someone whose model has to fit in a pocket.
days.recall: From memory: Day 67's three log items, and Day 66's credit-assignment sentence.
days.misconception: That learned always beats hardcoded. On a constrained device the honest question is which kind of mistake you can afford to make.
days.check: State the author's definition without notes, then give one task in this course where a rule beats a model.
days.gate: For three tasks on hardware you actually own, say rule or model - and defend the one where the answer is uncomfortable.
days.practice: `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py`. Then write the smallest task you could solve with a ten-line rule instead of a model, and actually write those ten lines in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/rule_vs_model.py`. Log which one you would trust and why.

days.title: One feature, one label: the shape of every training run
days.idea: The simplest trainable model in the book - predict emissions from engine displacement with a normalisation layer, a Sequential model, a compile step and `fit`. Read it for the pattern's shape, because every later model is the same five steps with more layers.
days.recall: From memory: Day 68's rule-or-model line, and the five-step shape itself.
days.misconception: That normalisation is housekeeping. A scale difference between inputs becomes a gradient difference, and the model learns whichever feature shouts.
days.check: Name the five steps in order and say which one a hand-written regression does not have.
days.gate: Replace the feature with something roughly a thousand times larger in scale, predict what happens to training, then run it and explain the result.
days.practice: Reproduce the pattern on data from `~/Desktop/ML/codes/frame.py`. If the framework is not installed here, do the same regression with the standard library in about 30 lines and note in your log that it was done without the library - that is allowed and is the stronger learning. Keep the five-step structure visible in the code.

days.title: TensorFlow Lite: the model is not one file
days.idea: Why a mobile book exists at all: TensorFlow Lite is the framework for running models on lower-powered devices - mobile, embedded, IoT - which means the trained model is only half the artefact. Conversion, quantisation and the runtime delegate are where the real constraints live.
days.recall: From memory: Day 69's five steps, and Day 67's service-history idea applied to a phone.
days.misconception: That a model is one file. The trained graph, the quantised weights and the delegate that executes them are three decisions with three different failure modes.
days.check: Say what quantisation trades away, in one sentence, and name the device class it is for.
days.gate: Take any model you trained this week and state precisely what you would give up to run it on the handset in your pocket.
days.practice: Find a model or notebook from your own work under `~/Desktop/ML/`, record its size in bytes, and estimate what an 8-bit version would weigh. No tooling required: a reasoned estimate is the exercise. Write the estimate and the reasoning in your log.

days.title: IoT data is a stream and it lies
days.idea: Two characteristics break the analytics assumptions at once: IoT data arrives continuously rather than as a table, and it is untrustworthy at the source - drift, dropped packets, clock skew. The book's own examples are remote patient monitoring and autonomous vehicles, so validity and latency come before accuracy.
days.recall: From memory: Day 70's three artefact decisions, and Day 21's data set-up steps.
days.misconception: That missing data is a cleaning problem. In a stream a gap is information about the device, and the right response may be an alert rather than an imputation.
days.check: Name the two characteristics the author identifies and the requirement each creates.
days.gate: Say which of your own scripts would break first if its input were a stream instead of a file, and exactly what it would do.
days.practice: `python3 ../iot-exercises/exercises/01_validate_sensor.py`. Then extend it so a stuck sensor reporting a constant 23.5 is a fault rather than valid data, and clock skew fails loudly instead of passing. Log both cases with the output.

days.title: Train in the cloud, infer at the edge
days.idea: The landscape chapter: which deep-learning frameworks are desktop-bound and which are cloud-bound, and the observation that most released libraries assume a machine far larger than an IoT node. Hence the practical split - heavy training off-device, light inference on it.
days.recall: From memory: Day 71's two characteristics, and Day 70's three artefact decisions.
days.misconception: That a framework choice is technical. On a 3.7GB laptop it is a budget choice, and pretending otherwise is how projects stall at installation.
days.check: Say which half of train-cloud / infer-edge you can do on this machine and which you cannot.
days.gate: Design the smallest IoT-shaped pipeline you could genuinely run here - one file as the data source, one training run that fits in memory, one rule at the edge - then say where the design becomes dishonest.
days.practice: Use `../iot-exercises/exercises/01_validate_sensor.py` as the edge stage and write a training stage in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/` that refuses to start if it would exceed 1GB. Measure with `/usr/bin/time -v python3 yourscript.py` and record the peak resident size of your largest run so far.

days.title: VITEC: reading a real paper end to end
days.idea: A complete research paper on violence detection from video, framed as feature extraction plus classification, with the honest difficulty being not the classifier but defining what a violent event looks like in continuous, noisy, socially judged data. Days 64 and 71 meet here in one application.
days.recall: From memory: Day 72's budget-versus-technical point, and Day 64's confident-and-wrong input.
days.misconception: That a published framework is a validated one. Read what the dataset was and where it came from before you believe the accuracy figure.
days.check: Name the dataset, the modality, and the one limitation the authors state about their own results.
days.gate: Say whether VITEC would work on a camera that cannot see the whole scene, and identify the assumption your answer rests on.
days.practice: Write a one-page reading in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/curriculum/aicon-vitec-notes.md`: claim, method, evidence, and the sentence where the authors hedge. Four short paragraphs, no quotation longer than a line.

days.title: The textbook definition, and the measure nobody has
days.idea: AGI as a system able to replicate or surpass human cognitive ability across varied and open-ended domains - followed by the admission that despite abundance of progress and interest, the field lacks a shared measure for the claim. This is the engineering account that Day 39's philosophical account could not give you.
days.recall: From memory: Day 39's reason the definition is contested, and Day 42's requirement for scoring a machine fairly.
days.misconception: That 'general' means 'very good at many things'. The load-bearing word in this definition is open-ended, which is a much stronger requirement.
days.check: Give the author's definition and name the word doing most of the work.
days.gate: Say how you would test for general rather than narrow-but-broad, and what you would need that you do not have.
days.practice: Search your own log for the first sentence you wrote defining AGI. Under it, write what this textbook adds: a measure, a mechanism, or a benchmark - and mark whichever of the three you cannot actually point to.

days.title: Solomonoff induction: the bound you cannot compute
days.idea: Sequence prediction that weights every computable hypothesis by its simplicity - Bayesian inference, Turing completeness and algorithmic information theory in one unimplementable object. Its value is as a yardstick: every practical model, including the transformer from Day 30, is measurably inadequate against it.
days.recall: From memory: Day 29's entropy as surprise, and Day 74's missing measure.
days.misconception: That Solomonoff induction is another algorithm. It is uncomputable; it is a bound. Reaching for it as a method is the mistake the chapter invites.
days.check: Say in one sentence why no program can compute it, and what practitioners approximate instead.
days.gate: Connect it to Day 29: state what complexity adds to the idea of surprise, in your own words.
days.practice: Write the shortest definition of 'the simplest explanation' you can defend in `~/Desktop/ML/codes/curriculum/solomonoff-notes.md`. Then apply it to one genuine ambiguity from this week and record which reading your definition picks and whether you agree with it.

days.title: Differentiable neurosymbolic inference: the interface is the hard part
days.idea: The hybrid architecture's core component - an engine that allows fluid interplay between discrete symbols and continuous representations, so logical reasoning can sit inside a trainable system. This is the concrete version of the argument Days 64-73 kept circling.
days.recall: From memory: Day 75's bound, and Day 68's rule-versus-model question.
days.misconception: That 'neurosymbolic' is a fusion which removes the difficulty. The engine must decide at every step what is symbol and what is gradient; the interface is the research problem, not the two halves.
days.check: Name the two representations the engine mediates and the one place they must not be confused.
days.gate: Give one task where the hybrid is obviously better than either pure side, and one where it is obviously worse.
days.practice: Write a 40-line version of the toy: parse explicit rules into data structures and answer a query by applying them, then note how long that took versus learning the same thing from examples. Start from `~/Desktop/ML/codes/mdlr/arithmetic.py`, which already encodes rules.

days.title: Catastrophic forgetting: why learning destroys
days.idea: One of the oldest problems in building AGI, stated plainly: learning a new task degrades previous knowledge, because sequential updates of shared parameters overwrite what made the old task work. Continual learning is the attempt to make updates additive rather than destructive.
days.recall: From memory: Day 76's interface problem, and Day 63's training-versus-working split.
days.misconception: That forgetting is a flaw of neural networks only. Your own study forgets on schedule, which is why this course puts recall questions before new material rather than after it.
days.check: Explain in one sentence why shared parameters cause the destruction.
days.gate: Name two mitigations, say what each costs, and say which one this course's spaced repetition is imitating.
days.practice: `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py`. Then train any small model from Day 63 on a second dataset and test whether it still performs on the first; record both numbers. Two tiny files are enough - do not load anything large on this machine.

days.title: What transformers can do, and what nobody claims
